item.title: An Imgur Celebration
item.description:
Hi everyone, I'm MrPuckett I celebrated my 41st birthday this week, but that's not why I'm excited today
Every year around my birthday is another celebration right here on Imgur
Tomorrow we're celebrating the SEVEN YEAR anniversary of TheFreePizzaDude! Over 17,000 meals sent to people in need since 2019!
I always love celebrating milestones for this project because it forces me to remember where I came from
I started TheFreePizzaDude 7 years ago with almost nothing I moved to a small Tennessee town after being homeless with only a dog and one suitcase I don't own or have a single thing today from 7 years ago, sadly not even the dog.
While everything was changing and every year brought new challenges in sobriety and life, only one thing has remained constant for me since 2019 Every week a bunch of wholesome strangers on the internet join me to send meals to people who are struggling
Even though it's only one day a week, it's given me the structure and hope that I needed most of my life No matter how good or how bad a day I had, I was only ever a few days away from being back here with friends across the world
So I hope you'll join us again this week to celebrate how much love (and cheese) has been shared over the last 7 years Saturday, 2pm central, @TheFreePizzaDude, let's party.
17,000+ meals, 1,500+ grocery orders, 22 different foster and adopted dogs on the posts One big day to celebrate it all
I remember the exact day 7 years ago when I first started the project, how little hope I had for such a beautiful future Tomorrow we'll look to send as much food, and as much hope as we can to people in need. ... If you can't make the post but still want to help, you can always contribute to the Meal Fund to help others get fed - https://www.paypal.me/TheFreePizzaDude https://ko-fi.com/thefreepizzadude ... Saturday, 2pm central, let's spread some love.

item.title: Ripley's bought my Etch A Sketch art!
item.description: I am thrilled to share that I've been working with Ripley's over the years which has led to many incredible adventures. So it means the world to me that they purchased my most ambitious Etch A Sketch series to date! If you visit the Grand Prairie location you can vote for my art through the end of the month which can in theory provide some extra capital for what I'm sure will be a Very Silly Pursuit :) Can't make it to Grand Prairie? Come see me in Orlando on Labor Day! I'll be making free art portraits with Ripley's from 2-4 at Icon Park. Can't make it to Orlando either? Ah well, hopefully you'll find a little placard about me and my art at a future Ripley's visit! Thank you all for the amazing support - the only reason Ripley's reached out to me was because I hit the front page of Reddit a few years ago. Sometimes upvotes really do matter, and I think that's pretty peachy keen.

item.title: Intense acting by Sidney Poitier in "Guess who's coming to dinner?" (1967) #REAL TALK
item.description: NOT SO FUN FACT: Spencer Tracy, who plays the white father was dying while the film was being shot. Co- star, Katherine Hepburn, and director, Stanley Kramer, both put up their salaries as backing because the studio didn't want to insure an actor who could possibly die in the middle of production. The very last scene in the film is the very last scene that Tracy appeared in; he died 17 days after it was filmed.

item.description: At least three sailors on the USS Abraham Lincoln have reportedly tried to jump into the ocean, but Trump says their deployment is "not nearly long enough." He has kept the carrier at sea for nine months fighting his Iran war, including a record 208 straight days without touching land. This week, crew member families broke their silence, describing meals of half a cup of rice and two tortillas, and weeks without hot water. When a reporter told Trump on Friday that they were worried, he said, "No, they're not." The Navy insists suicide attempts aboard have not risen. But on August 3, a rescue helicopter pulled a sailor from the sea. Trump promised the Lincoln will be swapped for "another very similar ship." His plan is one boat replacing another, with 5,000 people aboard whose families he refuses to hear. I've emailed 8,655 stories over 561 straight nights, free and without ads. item.title: Hand-Dug Caissons, 24 Feet Deep: Building a Pool Foundation on a Hollywood Hills Slope Nobody Thought Was Buildable.
item.description:
This is what we walked into before a single shovel hit the ground. Steep grade, dense growth, and a lot of unknowns. The first step was getting our team on-site to assess conditions. With soils testing underway and plans being developed, walking the site together helped us spot constraints, evaluate access, and coordinate the best path forward.
Drone shot of the slope before we broke ground. All of this would eventually be excavated to install a deep pile-supported foundation system. The hillside didn't look like much here.
Same angle after we cleared the vegetation. Clearing the site was the first major step, exposing the hillside, opening up access for our crew and revealing the space that would eventually become the project's centerpiece.
You can see just how much of the slope was basically unusable. Too steep to do anything with. The client knew they wanted to use this space; but weren't sure what was possible.
Temporary stairs in, plywood safety wall up, and the green pipe running down the hillside became our material chute, moving excavated soil straight into the bin. When there is no equipment access, you learn to work smarter.
Every one of these six piles was dug by hand, ranging from 15 to 24 feet deep depending on location. On terrain this steep, no heavy machinery could reach the site, so the crew dug the piles and dropped each rebar cage in by hand. A soils engineer verified each one. Together the piles support a cantilevered tie beam and footing system built for the above-ground pool shell.
Aerial view of the full row of piles lined up along the future retaining wall footprint. Every one of these is placed exactly per the engineered layout.
Grade beams formed up 8 feet above grade. Once the concrete is poured, they will create the flat, level base the pool will eventually sit on.
This is a shot of the concrete pour for the piles. Once this concrete cures, these become the primary load-bearing elements for the retaining walls, beams, and the pool.
Concrete going into the grade beams. That steel ties this beam directly into the piles below and the pool shell above. Everything is connected into one system.
Another pour shot, but you can see a sneak peek of the view and the reason why our client wants a pool up here.
Now for the shotcrete. This is how we form structural walls against a hillside. We use high-strength concrete sprayed under pressure, so it packs tight even on a vertical face.
After the shotcrete goes on, the wall gets smoothed out. Smooth surface, proper curing, built to last.
The base of the pool’s foundation is complete! The piles, grade beams, and retaining walls are all in. The exposed steel is capped and ready for the pool contractor to take over.
The foundation is in. This is the moment before it really starts to look like a pool.
Pool shell rebar and formwork going in. This ties the swimming pool structure directly into the foundation system we engineered and built.
Aerial of the same phase. You can really see here how everything ties back into the deep foundations below.
Concrete painted white to match the aesthetic of the home.
Pool shell, infinity edge, spa, and steps. All done. We didn't build this part, but all of it is sitting on the pile-supported system we engineered and built.
The client brought in a muralist to finish the space. This is the part where it starts to go from a construction site to a dream backyard.
Final drone shot. Pool filled, furniture in, mural complete. What was once a steep, unusable hillside is now a dream backyard oasis.
Here's the completed project. A huge thank you to our client, whose vision made this incredible space possible. Projects like this are built on collaboration, and it's been a pleasure to be part of the journey from concept to reality.
Our team got invited back to enjoy a quick dip in the very pool they helped build. Moments like this make all the hard work worth it. The clients are thrilled; we're thrilled. Job done. Want to see more start-to-finish structural projects like this? Drop a comment below and ask us anything about the engineering or construction process.
